new_statements.translation: p. 34: "Stress, which is predictable (it falls on the last syllable in isolated words), will not be marked in the transcriptions." — p. 192: "the location of stress is totally predictable: it falls on the last syllable of the word, and there is no morphological rule or lexical phonological rules that need information about the location of stress in the language." — p. 198: "The prosodic analysis of Mbyá indicates that the language shows final prominence. Stressed morphemes are nominal and verbal roots (235a-c) and derivational suffixes (235d-e). Unstressed morphemes are the inflectional suffixes and all prefixes" — p. 204: "Mbyá is a language with an iambic stress system, but one that stresses words formed by an iambic foot consisting only of two light syllables"

new_statements.relation_note: NOT in the 'works' list: already held by the project from the 2026-09-16 download pass, read here because the catalog had no quoted statement. Same placement as the catalog (final); adds the metrical analysis (iambic, quantity-sensitive, post-lexical), the morphological domain (root + derivational suffixes; inflection and prefixes unstressed) and the reported secondary stress. scanned of the txt renders 'cai' as 'caí' and 'acentual' as 'acentua!'; quotes above use the evident original spelling. Variety: Mbyá of Morro dos Cavalos and Maciambu, Paulo Lopes, Santa Catarina, Brazil.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress is fully predictable and falls on the last syllable of the (phonological) word; Martins analyses it as a post-lexical, right-headed iambic system (feet built left-to-right, End Rule right, no degenerate feet) in Hayes's framework. Roots and derivational suffixes are stress-bearing; inflectional suffixes and all prefixes are unstressed, so the final stressed syllable is the last syllable of the root or derivational complex (examples: ka.'ry, ka.va.'jú, a.ra.ra.'á, mboka-'í, -juka-uká). She calls the system quantity-sensitive because lengthened stressed monosyllables and word-final diphthongs form heavy syllables that attract stress, but these heavy syllables are always final, so placement stays final.
new_statements.secondary_stress: fn. 83, p. 201 (reporting others): "Meader (1961) propõe que no Mbyá, um grupo de ritmo com extensão de quatro ou mais sílabas toma um acento secundário. Guedes (1991:22) também afirma, tratando de palavras 'complexas', que ao se seguirem dois morfemas acentuados, os morfemas à esquerda têm em geral reduzida a intensidade de sua sílaba acentuada, mas sem que haja total apagamento" (Meader 1961: a rhythm group of four or more syllables takes a secondary stress; Guedes 1991: in complex words with two stressed morphemes in sequence, the left-hand morpheme's stressed syllable is reduced in intensity but not fully deleted). Martins's own grid marks one foot-level prominence per binary foot (a.ra.ra.'á).
new_statements.exceptions: Inflectional suffixes and prefixes are unstressed (invisible to stress); stressed monosyllables lengthen their vowel to satisfy a bimoraic minimal-word template; nasality is contrastive only in stressed syllables (tu'pã 'God' vs tu'pa 'bed', fn. 75); final-diphthong glide deletion in reduplicated disyllables is treated as a device that protects the oxytone pattern.
new_statements.identity_note: Martins 2003 describes the Mbyá of Morro dos Cavalos and Maciambu (Paulo Lopes, Santa Catarina, Brazil). Ivo 2018 covers four Guarani varieties of Brazil (Mbyá of SP/RJ/PR, Nhandewa of SP/PR, Nhandeva of MS, Kaiowá of MS) and phrases its stress rule for 'a língua Guarani' as a whole; its paroxytone-loan remark concerns the MS varieties only. de Paula 2016 describes Misiones Mbya (Argentina). Guedes 1987 describes the Mbiá of São Paulo state. The two Dooley works concern Brazilian Mbyá Guarani but were not opened.

The thesis covers four Brazilian Guarani varieties (Mbyá SP/RJ/PR, Nhandewa SP/PR, Nhandeva MS, Kaiowá MS) and states the stress rule for Guarani generally; no chapter or section is devoted to stress (stressed vs pretonic syllables are only a sampling variable for the acoustic study).
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is demarcative and assigned by rule to the last syllable of the root; in compounds only the rightmost root keeps its stress (mba'e + -ryru -> mba'eryru). Words are predominantly oxytone; the only paroxytones mentioned are Spanish loans in the Mato Grosso do Sul varieties (Kaiowá, Nhandeva), not Mbyá.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed; the first root of a compound is said to become pretonic (its stress lost), with no secondary stress mentioned.
new_statements.exceptions: Paroxytone loanwords from Spanish, admitted in the Mato Grosso do Sul varieties (Kaiowá/Nhandeva); stress statements are phrased for 'a língua Guarani' as a whole and hedged with 'predominantemente'.

sources.quote: No explicit stress-placement rule; concerns /h/-insertion and vowel reduplication in 'palavras monossilábicas acentuadas' (p.81-82: 'São reduplicados somente segmentos [+silábico] de palavras monossilábicas acentuadas'; unstressed suffix -py does not block it, stressed suffixes do). All phonetic transcriptions mark final stress ([ha'ku], [he'sa], [ainũ'pã mĩ'tã]). Summarises her 1983 Unicamp MA 'Subsídios para uma análise fonológica do Mbiá'.

A five-page article on two word-shape-conditioned rules (h-insertion, vowel reduplication in monosyllables); it never states where stress falls. It presupposes stress in passing: reduplication applies to 'uma palavra de uma só sílaba e acentuada' (a stressed monosyllabic word), is not blocked by 'um sufixo sem acento' (locative -py) but is blocked by 'sufixos acentuados' (intensive -rei [fe'i]); its phonetic transcriptions mark final stress throughout ([tãni'mbu], [i'po], [ho'o]).
